posts.description:
There's way too much hype about AI agents.

Here's your simple guide:

Forget the super complex taxonomies out there. There are 4 categories of tools you should know.

1. Consumer Agents

The latest LLMs, like Grok and Claude, have agents built-in. ChatGPT is rolling out the 'Agent' tool to paid plans as we speak.

These are best for:

- Ad-hoc analysis
- Quick research tasks
- Content creation (PRDs, strategy docs)

2. No-Code Agent Builders

There is a new class of tools that you must know. Tools like Zapier and Lindy offer where you can do things like connecting your Gmail to Claude.

Be sure to explore these for:

- Email triage
- Competitor monitoring
- Automated data reporting

3. Developer-First Platforms

All the tools you've heard like CrewAI, Langchain, and Autogen are great frameworks for developers. Think of them as the React/Node for agents.

They're for:

- Customer-facing agents
- Deep system integrations
- Complex, proprietary business logic

4. Specialized Agent Apps

Tools like Cursor, Otter, and Jasper are specialized agent apps. They're supported by complex business logic to do one task really well.

My recommendations:

- Coding → Cursor
- Meetings → Otter AI
- Research → Perplexity

Ready to go the layer deeper? I teamed up with AI PM at Meta Vikash Rungta to write you the web's most practical and simple guide: https://lnkd.in/eeey5Cxr

Please, let's end all the hype and talk real use cases.

P.S. What agent are you using most?

comments.author: Lewin Wanzer
comments.text:
Thanks for sharing, Aakash. Appreciate the breakdown—but here’s the twist most are missing: the AI agent is Agent Smith.
The more we chase “smart tasks” without structure, the more we lose the plot. Developers are confused. “AI Architects” don’t exist. And agents are now doing things they were never cleared to do.
We don’t need more tools—we need orchestration, identity-bound execution, and governed outcomes. Tourque will set the standard. Until that’s the norm, it’s just hype on autopilot.
